raw:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out what would happen next after the farmers in Wyoming hunted and got rid of the hawks that were preying on their chickens. The options are A) Chicken population goes down, B) Mice and rats increase, C) Another bird of prey replaces the hawk, D) Chickens have lower disease rate.

First, I think about what happens when you remove a predator. In this case, the hawks were hunting the chickens. If the hawks are gone, maybe the chickens won't be as stressed, so they might not die as much. That could mean the chicken population might actually go up, but option A says it would go down, which doesn't make sense to me.

Then, thinking about option B, mice and rats. Sometimes when predators are removed, other animals can take over their role. Hawks eat small animals like mice, so without hawks, maybe mice and rats would have more predators? Or maybe the chickens could eat them. I'm not sure if their population would increase or decrease.

Option C says another bird of prey would replace the hawk. That makes sense because in ecosystems, if one predator is removed, another might move in to take its place. So maybe another bird like a falcon or eagles might come to hunt the chickens. That would mean the chickens are still at risk, but from a different predator.

Option D, chickens having lower disease. I don't see how removing hawks would affect the chickens' health. Diseases are more about their environment, food, or other chicken-related issues, not the predators.

So, putting it all together, the most logical next step is that another bird of prey would replace the hawks. That seems to fit with how ecosystems usually work, where another predator might take over when one is removed. So I think the answer is C.
